stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Food regulators in several countries permit a "reduced fat" label on any product containing at least 25 percent less fat than its standard version. The rule was meant to steer calorie-conscious shoppers toward lighter foods. Nutrition researcher Ilse Marten notes, however, that manufacturers often restore the flavor lost with the fat by adding sugar or starch, so that many labeled products contain nearly as many calories as the originals. Consequently, the label may ______
choices: persuade most shoppers that added sugar is a healthier ingredient than fat is.
lead shoppers to buy products with more calories than the standard versions contain.
steer shoppers who use it to cut calories toward foods that barely help them do so.
lead shoppers who ignore nutrition labels to eat more fat than they did before.
explanation: The label's goal is to help calorie-conscious shoppers, but the products it marks have nearly as many calories as the originals. The unintended effect lands on the group the rule was meant to help: the shoppers who trust the label get foods that do little to lower their calories.

A.why: You added a belief the passage never mentions. Nothing suggests shoppers decide sugar is healthier, and "most" is a strength the text can't support.

B.why: You fell for strength creep. The passage says "nearly as many" calories, not more. The labeled products come close to the originals but are never said to exceed them.

D.why: You pinned the harm on the wrong group. The rule was aimed at shoppers who read labels, and the passage says nothing about people who ignore them or about how much fat they eat.

subtype_name: Name the mismatch or unintended effect

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Baroque keyboard scores often look sparse: a single bass line with a few numerals written beneath it. Early modern students of the repertoire took this sparseness as a sign that the pieces were easy to play. Musicologist Tomás Ruelas argues the reverse. The numerals, he shows, told performers which harmonies to improvise in real time above the bass, a skill that took years of training to master. There is thus a disparity between ______
choices: how little of the music the page records and how much the performer was expected to supply.
how easy the pieces were to play and how complicated their notation looked.
how hard the pieces were to perform and how long improvisation took to learn.
the harmonies composers intended and the harmonies performers chose to play.
explanation: The two sides are a page that records very little (a bass line and numerals) and a performer who must improvise full harmonies on top of it. The disparity is between what is written down and what the player has to provide.

B.why: You reversed the contrast. The notation looks simple and the playing is hard, not the other way around.

C.why: You paired two things from the same side. Hard performance and long training both describe the demanding half, so the simple-looking notation is missing and no disparity is named.

D.why: You invented a conflict. The passage never says performers departed from what composers intended. It says the numerals told them which harmonies to improvise.

subtype_name: Name the mismatch or unintended effect

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Earthen levees are built along rivers to reduce the damage floods cause to nearby communities. Hydrologists have long observed, however, that land behind a new levee tends to attract homes and businesses, since it is now regarded as safe. Each levee is designed to withstand floods only up to a specified size, and larger floods, though rare, still occur. Consequently, a levee may ______
choices: fail during the ordinary floods that it was specifically designed to hold back.
shift the floods it prevents upstream onto communities located farther downstream.
protect the new homes and businesses behind it from most of the river's floods.
increase the amount of property exposed to floods larger than it can withstand.
explanation: The levee is meant to reduce flood damage, but it draws new building onto land that is still at risk from rare, larger floods. So it can increase the amount of property those big floods would damage, which is the opposite of its goal.

A.why: You ignored the design limit. The passage says levees hold up to their specified size. The risk comes from rarer, larger floods, not ordinary ones.

B.why: You added an extra step. Downstream effects may be real in some places, but the passage never mentions them. Its argument is entirely about building behind the levee.

C.why: You stated only one side of the tension. Protection from most floods is the levee's intended benefit. The question asks what follows from the gap between that safety and the rare large flood.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Nineteenth-century collectors who transcribed oral folktales saw themselves as rescuing a tradition from disappearance. Folklorist Maren Aalto observes that oral tales had survived precisely by changing, since each teller adapted plot and detail to the audience at hand. Once a printed version circulated in a region, however, villagers increasingly treated it as the correct telling and corrected storytellers who departed from it. The unintended effect of the collectors' work was thus to ______
choices: preserve tales that would otherwise have been forgotten within a generation.
weaken the very variability that had allowed the tradition to survive.
make villagers lose interest in hearing tales performed by local storytellers.
encourage tellers to adapt printed tales more freely to suit their audiences.
explanation: The collectors wanted to keep the tradition alive, and Aalto says it survived by varying. Print made one version the "correct" one and discouraged variation, so the collectors undermined the thing that had kept the tradition going.

A.why: You gave the intended goal, not the unintended effect. Preservation is what the collectors hoped for, and "within a generation" is a claim the passage never makes.

C.why: You went beyond the text. Villagers kept listening closely enough to correct tellers, so nothing shows they lost interest.

D.why: You reversed the effect. Villagers corrected tellers who departed from the printed version, which discouraged free adaptation.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: A city offered free flu vaccinations at clinics open only on weekday mornings, aiming to narrow the gap in vaccination rates between its low-income residents and everyone else. Clinic records showed that most people who came were retirees and salaried workers with flexible schedules, few of whom were low-income. Hourly workers, who make up most of the city's low-income population, rarely attended. As a result, the program may have ______
choices: overburdened clinics with more retirees and salaried workers than staff could serve.
led hourly workers to distrust health programs that are run by the city.
lowered vaccination rates among low-income residents below their earlier level.
widened rather than narrowed the gap it was designed to close.
explanation: The program set out to close a gap, but most of the people it vaccinated were not low-income. Raising rates mainly among people already better off would make the gap wider, the opposite of the goal. "May have" matches how cautious the evidence is.

A.why: You looked at the side the program already favoured. The passage never mentions staffing problems, and the question is about the group the program was meant to protect.

B.why: You added a motive. Hourly workers stayed away because of the hours, as far as the passage shows. Nothing points to distrust.

C.why: You fell for strength creep. A program that failed to reach low-income residents doesn't lower their rate below where it was. It only fails to raise it.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Backyard bird feeding is often promoted as a way to support declining songbird populations. A survey by ornithologist Priya Venn found, however, that the birds visiting feeders most often were house sparrows and other common generalist species, while several declining insect-eating species almost never used feeders at all. The generalists also compete with those declining species for scarce nest cavities. People who feed birds in order to help vulnerable species therefore risk ______
choices: strengthening the competitors of the very species they mean to help.
depriving common generalist species of food they need in order to survive.
driving declining insect-eating species to abandon their nest sites entirely.
drawing declining species to feeders where too few insects are available.
explanation: Feeders mostly feed the generalists, and the generalists compete with the declining species for nest cavities. So people trying to help vulnerable birds end up supporting those birds' competitors, which hurts the group they meant to protect.

B.why: You aimed the harm at the wrong side, and in the wrong direction. Generalists are the birds feeders benefit most, not birds that lose food.

C.why: You fell for strength creep. Competition for cavities doesn't establish that the declining species abandon their nests "entirely."

D.why: You missed a stated detail. The declining species almost never use feeders, so feeders don't draw them anywhere.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Linguists documenting endangered languages increasingly rely on audio recordings, which are inexpensive to make and easy to archive. Yet a recording captures only what speakers happen to say. It cannot show whether a rare construction is ungrammatical or merely unused. Settling that question requires lengthy sessions in which a trained linguist asks speakers to judge invented sentences, and few fluent speakers of most endangered languages remain. Thus there is a disparity between ______
choices: the number of recordings linguists make and the number they can archive.
the sentences speakers say naturally and the sentences they judge acceptable.
the evidence that is easiest to gather and the evidence some questions require.
the low cost of making recordings and the effort of transcribing them accurately.
explanation: Recordings are cheap and easy to collect, but they can't answer questions about grammaticality. Those need judgment sessions, which are slow and depend on speakers who are scarce. The disparity is between the evidence that is easy to get and the evidence certain questions actually need.

A.why: You built a gap the passage rules out. Recordings are described as easy to archive, so making and archiving them aren't in tension.

B.why: You paired the wrong two things. The passage contrasts two kinds of evidence, not speakers' speech with their judgments, and it never says those two differ.

D.why: You matched only one side. Cheap recordings are in the passage, but transcription never is. The real other side is the scarce judgment sessions.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Land managers in parts of the American West have used controlled burns to clear sagebrush, hoping to reduce the fuel available to large wildfires. Ecologist Ruth Calder reports that on burned plots, invasive cheatgrass, which dries out early each summer and ignites easily, often established itself faster than the sagebrush could regrow. Her findings suggest that in these areas, controlled burns may ______
choices: eliminate sagebrush permanently from every plot on which they are used.
favor the very vegetation that makes wildfires more likely to start.
reduce the fuel available to wildfires for many years after each burn.
fail because cheatgrass is more resistant to fire than sagebrush is.
explanation: The burns are meant to reduce wildfire fuel, but they let in cheatgrass, which dries early and catches fire easily. So the burns can encourage plants that make fires more likely. "Suggest" and "may" fit this hedged claim.

A.why: You fell for strength creep. Cheatgrass establishing "faster than" sagebrush regrows doesn't mean sagebrush is gone "permanently" from "every" plot.

C.why: You gave only the policy's goal. Calder's findings point the other way: the burns may replace sagebrush with a more flammable fuel.

D.why: You reversed the trait. The passage says cheatgrass ignites easily, which is the opposite of fire-resistant.
